items.title: OpenRouter – "Requests you sent to MiniMax models may have been read"
items.summary: Got this email from OpenRouter today: A security researcher placed unique test URLs in prompts sent to MiniMax models from July to October 2026. A third party accessed those URLs 40 to 130 hours after the requests were sent, whether MiniMax served a request directly or another provider forwarded it to MiniMax. With one exception, the same tests on other models at those providers were not accessed, and none of the AWS test keys were used. Your account sent 21 requests to MiniMax models through MiniMax, Novita, StreamLake and AtlasCloud, from June 22 at 03:02 to July 3 at 23:28 UTC.

items.title: OpenRouter prompts to Minimax may have been read
items.summary: I received the following email from OpenRouter and it appears authentic. There is no public page or blog post. -- Title: Requests you sent to MiniMax models may have been read Hi there, A security researcher placed unique test URLs in prompts sent to MiniMax models from July to October 2026. A third party accessed those URLs 40 to 130 hours after the requests were sent, whether MiniMax served a request directly or another provider forwarded it to MiniMax. With one exception, the same tests on other models at those providers were not accessed, and none of the AWS test keys were used.

deep.body: I received the following email from OpenRouter and it appears authentic. There is no public page or blog post. -- Title: Requests you sent to MiniMax models may have been read Hi there, A security researcher placed unique test URLs in prompts sent to MiniMax models from July to October 2026. A third party accessed those URLs 40 to 130 hours after the requests were sent, whether MiniMax served a request directly or another provider forwarded it to MiniMax. With one exception, the same tests on other models at those providers were not accessed, and none of the AWS test keys were used. Your account sent [redacted] requests to MiniMax models through MiniMax and Novita, from [redacted] to [redacted] UTC. AtlasCloud, Novita and StreamLake have told us they forwarded OpenRouter requests for MiniMax models to MiniMax. Based on what the researcher and these providers have reported, the issue sits with MiniMax and the providers that forwarded to it, not with OpenRouter. We are passing on what they have told us. MiniMax told StreamLake that content moderation was enabled on its endpoints before October 22 and that it has since enabled Zero Data Retention. We have asked MiniMax for its own account and have not received one. This means a third party may have read the prompts and outputs of these requests. While we investigate, we have removed the Zero Data Retention label from these MiniMax-model endpoints.

comments.text: I have received the same email. (and for posterity, I have no affiliation with MiniMax)

items.title: How do we get 1 TW a year of orbital compute by 2035?
items.summary: - 50k Starship V4 launches a year, each carrying 200 t (20 MW of compute). That’s 137 a day, one every 2 minutes in two windows of roughly 5–7am and 5–7pm local. As Earth spins, the launch site passes under that target orbit twice a day, at local dawn and local dusk. Globally we’re at about 1 launch a day right now. - The always-sunlit orbit needs launches heading north or south over open water. On US coasts only south works, and packing every usable spot with Starship pads gets us to just 25–30 launches a day. We need 5× that. - So we will go out to sea, 300 km off central California.

items.title: Should Uber Ratings Decay over Time?
items.summary: I’ve been thinking about how platforms like Uber calculate reputation scores, and I believe there’s a fundamental flaw in how historical ratings are treated. Uber calculates passenger ratings using the last 500 rated trips, regardless of when those trips occurred. In my case, I have 455 ratings, 426 of which are five stars (93.6%). My overall rating is 4.86. What bothers me isn’t the score itself, but the underlying methodology. A negative rating from five years ago can carry exactly the same weight as one received yesterday.

items.title: This Industrial Revolution Belongs to the Builders
items.summary: You've heard AI = Labor. Therefore Labor -> 0. Some people think this means that only asset owners, people with lots of capital, will come out ahead. They're wrong. Because as a builder/founder, you create value. Capital must capture some of this value to have a return. The reason founders primarily need capital is to pay for labor (either employees or supplier overhead). So this means that Capital ~= Labor.

deep.body: You've heard AI = Labor. Therefore Labor -> 0. Some people think this means that only asset owners, people with lots of capital, will come out ahead. They're wrong. Because as a builder/founder, you create value. Capital must capture some of this value to have a return. The reason founders primarily need capital is to pay for labor (either employees or supplier overhead). So this means that Capital ~= Labor. But that's a problem for the "owners of capital will own everything" narrative, because now we have: AI = Labor = Capital -> 0 In practice this will happen slowly as builders need less and less capital to build, capital will increasingly struggle to capture value created by builders. Counterintuitively this means valuations will climb dramatically reflecting capital paying more and more to capture less and less value from builders. As disruption accelerates, volatility increases while broader market wide returns start to stagnate. The net will be a wholesale wealth and power transfer from capital holders to builders/founders, on the magnitude of what happened between the aristocracy and the capitalist class in the earlier industrial revolutions. It's already started, companies are raising later and at higher valuations. Most people accept that if superintelligence were created, capital would be useless, but what they often don't realize is that a class of builders armed with AI is already creating a distributed superintelligence that will have the same effect. Interested if anyone else shares this perspective.

Elite builders (programmers) who can leverage AI and build products everyone needs. They are more like rock stars. 3. Deep state people who control military and intelligence, because violence always gets its share. 4. Auxiliary interest groups like some politicians, some other big capitals, etc. Everyone else gets screwed. Oh, someone might be lucky enough to be the Mafia of the underworld, because there gotta be someone who maintains law and order.

> Because as a builder/founder, you create value. Through labor. It seems like you're saying that builders/founders are a special kind of labor that AI cannot replace. Why do you think you're so special?

I think it’s more like marketers will own the future. If the cost of building stuff gets closer and closer to zero, then the valuable skill is getting attention. In a crowded market, the objective is to stand out.
builders are getting commoditized, anyone can build. this era belongs to those who champion distribution
